To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
N-glycosylated HBV envelope proteins are synthesized in a cotranslitional manner, but that the large envelope protein L can be modified with N-linked glycans in a posttranslational manner.
the HBV envelope proteins are subject to posttranslatory N-glycosylations and that the N-glicans are not necessary for the virus assembly.

the large L envelope protein of hepatitis B virus is N-glycosylated at two sites, namely, at asparagine 4 and 113, and that these N-glycans can be added to L both cotranslationally and posttranslationally.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the posttranslatalional modification of a viral glycoprotein and its impact on virus morphogenesis.
the identification and characterization of novel L isoforms, which are due to post-translational N-gylcosylation.
the identification and characterization of posttranslational glycosylated isoforms of the HBV large L envelope protein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the posttranslitional N-glycosylations of HBV L are dispensable for virion morphogenesis but are essential for the release of the virions.
HBV is able to utilize both cotranslational and posttranslational mechanisms for N-glycosylating L.
the HBV L protein is subject to co- and posttranslational glycosylation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
N-glycans on HBV envelope proteins do not play an essential role for HBV morphogeneses.
HBV has a unique N-glycosylated envelope protein and a novel mechanism of glycan addition.
N-glycosylated L is not required for HBV morphogenic process but rather for the release of virions by inhibiting the cell glycoprotein functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the N-glycerosylation of L is not a prerequisite for HBV assembly and secretion.
posttranslational glycan addition to a protein can be used to generate isoforms that are not only of interest to basic science, but can also be of value for diagnostics and vaccine development.
posttranslational protein modification is not restricted to the secretory pathway but can occur on cytoplasmic proteins.
